questions.q: Convert the binary numeral 1011010 to decimal.
Convert 523 (decimal) to binary.
questions.explain: Largest power of 2 that fits in 523 is 512 = 2^9, leaving 11 = 8 + 2 + 1. So 523 = 2^9 + 2^3 + 2^1 + 2^0 = 1000001011.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the binary numeral 10011?
Using the 'largest power of 2 that fits' method, convert 100 (decimal) to binary.
questions.explain: 64 fits (remainder 36), 32 fits (remainder 4), 4 fits (remainder 0). 100 = 2^6 + 2^5 + 2^2 = 1100100.

questions.q: In a positional numeral system, what does the digit at position i (counting from the right, starting at 0) encode?
choices: How many copies of base^i are added to the value
How many copies of i are added to the value
How many copies of i^base are added to the value
The exponent the base is raised to
questions.explain: Value = sum of d_i * base^i. The digit d_i says how many copies of base^i to add. The method itself works for any base.

questions.q: In a positional numeral system, the base is:
choices: The number of distinct digit symbols (including 0)
The largest digit value
The number of digits in the numeral
Always 10
questions.explain: A positional system has a fixed set of digit symbols including 0, and the base is the number of symbols. Base 10 has 0-9; base 2 has 0 and 1.

questions.q: Using n = 8 bits, what is the largest unsigned integer that can be represented?
questions.explain: n bits represent the unsigned integers 0 ... 2^n - 1. For n = 8 that is 2^8 - 1 = 255.

questions.q: How many bits does it take to write 7053 as an unsigned binary numeral (no leading zeros)?
questions.explain: 2^12 = 4096 <= 7053 < 8192 = 2^13, so the highest position is 12 and the numeral has 13 bits: 1101110001101.

questions.q: The written symbol '17' is itself the number seventeen.
questions.explain: '17' is a numeral, an agreed-upon code that represents the number seventeen. The same number could be written in other codes, such as 10001 in binary or XVII in Roman numerals.

questions.q: Why do computers need algorithms for converting between decimal and binary?
choices: Only to interact with humans, who read and write base 10, while the computer represents and processes everything in base 2
Because the ALU can only add decimal numbers
Because memory stores numbers in decimal and the CPU works in binary
Because binary cannot represent negative numbers
questions.explain: Inside the computer everything is binary. Conversions exist only so the computer can take input from and show output to humans who use base 10.

questions.q: Add the 4-bit numbers 1001 + 0101. Give the 4-bit result.
questions.explain: Working right to left with carries: 1+1 = 0 carry 1; 0+0+1 = 1; 0+1 = 1; 1+0 = 1. Result 1110 (9 + 5 = 14), and there is no carry out of the MSB, so no overflow.

questions.q: Adding 1011 + 0111 in a 4-bit system produces:
choices: 0010, with a carry of 1 out of the MSB (overflow)
10010, stored in full
1110, with no overflow
0010, with no carry out of the MSB
questions.explain: 11 + 7 = 18 = 10010. Only 4 bits fit, so the stored result is 0010. The addition of the two MSBs generated a carry of 1, which is the unsigned overflow.

questions.q: Compute 0111 + 1110 in a 4-bit system, ignoring overflow. Give the 4 stored bits.
questions.explain: 0111 + 1110 = 10101. The 5th (overflow) bit is dropped, leaving 0101. As unsigned values: (7 + 14) mod 16 = 5.

questions.q: What is the LSB of a binary number?
choices: The least significant bit, the right-most bit
The least significant bit, the left-most bit
The last signed bit, the left-most bit
The lowest set bit, the right-most 1
questions.explain: LSB = least significant bit (right-most, weight 2^0). MSB = most significant bit (left-most). Binary addition starts at the LSBs and moves toward the MSBs.

questions.q: In unsigned n-bit binary addition, when does overflow happen?
choices: When adding the two most significant bits (plus the incoming carry) produces a carry of 1
When the two least significant bits are both 1
When any column produces a carry
Whenever the result has a 1 in its MSB
questions.explain: If the last bit-wise addition (at the MSBs) produces a carry of 1, the true sum needs n+1 bits and has overflowed. Carries in lower columns are normal and just move to the next column.

questions.q: Dropping the overflow bit of an n-bit addition is the binary equivalent of computing the sum modulo 2^n.
questions.explain: The dropped bit has weight 2^n, so throwing it away is the same as subtracting 2^n, which gives the sum mod 2^n.

questions.q: In a single column of multi-bit binary addition, what is the maximum number of bits being added together?
questions.explain: Each column adds the two bits in that position plus the carry from the previous column. That is why a full adder (3-bit adder) is the building block for multi-bit adders.

questions.q: Addition is described as the foundation of all arithmetic. Which of these operations are obtained from addition?
choices: Subtraction (by adding the negation)
Multiplication
Division
Bitwise And
questions.explain: Subtraction comes 'for free' as x + (-y) in two's complement. Multiplication and division can be implemented efficiently using addition. Bitwise And is a separate logic operation computed directly by And gates.

questions.q: The same binary addition algorithm works for any word size n (16, 32, 64, ...).
questions.explain: Adding right to left and propagating carries is the same procedure whatever n is. Adding two n-bit numbers is just more of the same.

questions.q: In an n-bit two's complement system, how is -x coded (for x != 0)?
choices: As the binary code of 2^n - x
As the binary code of 2^(n-1) - x
As x with its MSB set to 1
As !x (all bits of x flipped)
questions.explain: The two's complement of x is 2^n - x, and that is the code for -x. Setting the MSB is sign-magnitude, which was rejected. Flipping the bits alone gives -x - 1.

questions.q: Give the 5-bit two's complement code for -2.
What decimal value does the 4-bit two's complement code 1011 represent?
questions.explain: The MSB is 1, so the value is negative: -(2^4 - 1011) = -(16 - 11) = -5.

questions.q: What range of integers can n bits represent in two's complement?
questions.explain: That gives 2^n values in total. For n = 4 the range is -8 ... 7, so there is one more negative number than positive. (0 ... 2^n - 1 is the unsigned range.)

questions.q: What is the most negative number representable in 16-bit two's complement?
Negate the 8-bit two's complement code 01011000 (88). Give the 8-bit result.
questions.explain: Flip all bits: 10100111, then add 1: 10101000. Another shortcut: keep the trailing 0s and the first 1 from the right (1000), then flip the rest (0101 becomes 1010). Check: 256 - 88 = 168 = 10101000.

questions.q: Which shortcut for computing -x from the code of x is easiest to implement in hardware?
choices: Flip all the bits of x, then add 1
Flip all the bits of x
Flip only the MSB of x
Shift x left one position, then flip the MSB
questions.explain: Negation is 'flip all bits and add 1'. Flipping alone gives -x - 1. Flipping only the MSB is sign-magnitude thinking and does not work in two's complement.

questions.q: Compute (-2) + (-3) in 4-bit two's complement. Give the 4-bit result.
questions.explain: 1110 + 1101 = 11011. Dropping the overflow bit leaves 1011, the code for -5. Plain bit-wise addition works without knowing which operands are negative.

questions.q: In 4-bit two's complement, compute 4 + (-7). What decimal value does the result represent?
questions.explain: -7 is coded as 16 - 7 = 9. Then 4 + 9 = 13, and 13 mod 16 = 13 = 1101, the code for -3.

questions.q: Which of these 4-bit two's complement additions overflow (give a wrong signed result)?
questions.explain: 5 + 7 gives 1100 = -4: two positives produced a negative. -7 + -3 gives (1)0110 = 6: two negatives produced a positive. 6 + -2 = 0100 = 4 and -2 + -5 = 1001 = -7 are correct, even though both produce a carry out that is discarded.

questions.q: How do you detect overflow when adding two's complement numbers?
choices: Adding two positives gives a negative result, or adding two negatives gives a positive result
A carry comes out of the MSB
The result is negative
The two operands have different signs
questions.explain: A carry out of the MSB is not a reliable sign: 6 + (-2) produces one and is still correct. Overflow is shown when the result's sign is wrong given the operands' signs. Operands with different signs can never overflow.

questions.q: Why was the sign-magnitude scheme (MSB = sign, other bits = magnitude) rejected in favor of two's complement?
choices: It has two codes for zero (+0 and -0)
code(x) + code(-x) != code(0)
The codes do not increase monotonically with x
It cannot represent any negative numbers
It needs n+1 bits to store an n-bit value
questions.explain: Sign-magnitude has a -0, its codes for x and -x do not add to code(0), and its codes are not monotonic, so it needs extra hardware. Two's complement fixes all three problems.

questions.q: With two's complement, arithmetic on signed integers can be done by the same hardware that does arithmetic on unsigned integers.
questions.explain: Signed addition is just regular addition modulo 2^n, the same bit-wise operation. That is the main reason two's complement is used.

questions.q: How is x - y computed in a two's complement system?
choices: As x + (-y), where -y is obtained by flipping y's bits and adding 1
With a dedicated subtractor circuit using borrow bits
As x + !y
As !x + !y
questions.explain: x - y = x + (-y), and negation is flip-and-add-1, so subtraction needs no hardware beyond an adder. x + !y is off by one: it equals x - y - 1.

questions.q: What is the 16-bit two's complement code for -1?
questions.explain: 2^16 - 1 = 65535 = sixteen 1s. Equivalently, flip 0000000000000001 to get 1111111111111110, then add 1.

questions.q: In two's complement, every positive number's code starts with 0 and every negative number's code starts with 1.
questions.explain: The MSB works as a sign indicator, which is why the ALU's ng output can be read straight from the MSB of out.

questions.q: In 4-bit two's complement, what do you get by applying 'flip all bits, then add 1' to 1000 (-8)?
choices: 1000 (still -8), because +8 is outside the 4-bit range
questions.explain: Flipping 1000 gives 0111, and adding 1 gives 1000. The 4-bit range is -8 ... 7, so +8 cannot be represented and the negation overflows back to -8.

questions.q: The HalfAdder's two outputs are identical to which standard gates?
choices: sum = Xor(a, b), carry = And(a, b)
sum = Or(a, b), carry = And(a, b)
sum = Xor(a, b), carry = Or(a, b)
sum = And(a, b), carry = Xor(a, b)
questions.explain: Truth table: 0+0 = 00, 0+1 = 01, 1+0 = 01, 1+1 = 10 (carry, sum). sum is 1 when exactly one input is 1 (Xor), and carry is 1 only when both are 1 (And).

questions.q: A FullAdder gets a = 1, b = 0, c = 1. What are its outputs?
choices: sum = 0, carry = 1
sum = 1, carry = 0
sum = 1, carry = 1
sum = 0, carry = 0
questions.explain: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 = binary 10. sum is the LSB (0) and carry is the MSB (1).

questions.q: A FullAdder with a = b = c = 1 outputs sum = 1 and carry = 1.
questions.explain: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = binary 11, so sum (LSB) = 1 and carry (MSB) = 1.

questions.q: A FullAdder can be built from two HalfAdders plus one more simple gate that combines the two half-adder carries. Which gate is it?
choices: Or
And
Not
Nand
questions.explain: HA1 adds a and b, giving s1 and c1. HA2 adds s1 and c, giving sum and c2. The final carry is 1 if either half adder produced a carry: carry = Or(c1, c2). (c1 and c2 are never both 1, so Xor would also work, but Or is the natural choice.)

questions.q: How can an n-bit adder be built?
choices: As an array of full adders, each one's carry feeding the next more-significant position
As n half adders working independently with no connections between them
As n Xor gates, one per bit position
As one full adder applied to all n bits at once
questions.explain: Each step adds three bits (two input bits plus the incoming carry) and passes its carry up the significance ladder from the LSB to the MSB.

questions.q: Why is the straightforward multi-bit adder slow, and what technique addresses this?
choices: The carry must ripple from the LSB pair to the MSB pair; carry look-ahead logic reduces the delay
The bits must be added one at a time by a clock; pipelining fixes it
Xor gates are slow; replacing them with Nand gates fixes it
Overflow detection takes time; ignoring overflow fixes it
questions.explain: The column additions run in parallel, but each carry depends on the previous column, so there is a long propagation delay. Carry look-ahead techniques reduce it. Addition is so common that this kind of speedup improves performance across the whole computer.

questions.q: In a 16-bit adder, the bit-wise additions are computed in parallel, while the carry propagation happens sequentially.
questions.explain: Every column's gates are wired at the same time, but a column's correct output depends on the carry from the column to its right, so carries settle one after another.

questions.q: Which single HDL part correctly implements Inc16 (out = in + 1)?
choices: Add16(a=in, b[0]=true, out=out);
Add16(a=in, b=true, out=out);
Add16(a=in, b[15]=true, out=out);
Add16(a=in, b=false, out=out);
questions.explain: b[0]=true sets only the LSB, and unassigned bits default to 0, so b = 0000000000000001. b=true sets all 16 bits (= -1), which makes out = in - 1. b[15]=true adds -32768, and b=false adds 0.

questions.q: Inc16 receives in = 1111111111111111. What is out (16 bits)?
questions.explain: 1111111111111111 + 1 = 1 0000000000000000. The carry out of the MSB is ignored, so out is all 0s. In two's complement this is -1 + 1 = 0.

questions.q: How do the Add16 and Inc16 chips handle overflow?
choices: It is neither detected nor handled; the most significant carry is simply dropped
It is detected and reported on an extra 1-bit output
The result is clamped to the largest representable value
The chip outputs all 1s to signal an error
questions.explain: Both chips do integer two's complement addition with overflow neither detected nor handled. Dropping the carry gives addition mod 2^16, which is exactly what signed two's complement arithmetic needs.

questions.q: In what order does the Hack ALU apply its control bits?
choices: zx then nx on x, and zy then ny on y; then f selects x+y or x&y; then no optionally negates the output
nx then zx on x, and ny then zy on y; then f; then no
f first, then zx/nx/zy/ny on the result, then no
no first, then f, then zx/nx/zy/ny
questions.explain: Presetting: zero, then negate, each input. Compute: f = 1 gives x+y, f = 0 gives x&y. Postsetting: no = 1 gives out = !out. The order matters, since zeroing then negating is how the ALU makes all 1s (-1).

questions.q: The Hack ALU has six 1-bit control inputs. How many different functions could these bits potentially select?
questions.explain: 2^6 = 64 combinations. Only 18 of them give the documented, useful functions (0, 1, -1, x, y, !x, !y, -x, -y, x+1, y+1, x-1, y-1, x+y, x-y, y-x, x&y, x|y).

questions.q: Which control bits (zx nx zy ny f no, as a 6-character string) make the Hack ALU compute x+y?
questions.explain: Leave x and y unchanged (zx = nx = zy = ny = 0), pick addition (f = 1), and do not negate the output (no = 0).

questions.q: What does the Hack ALU compute with control bits 001110 (zx nx zy ny f no)?
choices: -x
!x
questions.explain: x is unchanged. y is zeroed and then negated, giving 111...1 = -1. f = 1 adds: x + (-1). no = 0 leaves the result as is, so out = x - 1.

questions.q: What does the Hack ALU compute with control bits 111111?
questions.explain: x becomes !0 = -1 and y becomes !0 = -1. f = 1 gives -1 + -1 = -2 = 111...10. no = 1 flips that to 000...01 = 1.

questions.q: The control bits 010101 make the ALU compute x|y. Which identity makes this work?
choices: x|y = !(x & y)
x|y = !x + !y
questions.explain: nx = 1 and ny = 1 negate both inputs, f = 0 Ands them, and no = 1 negates the result: !(!x & !y), which equals x|y by De Morgan's law.

questions.q: x = 30, y = 20, and the control bits are 000111 (zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=1 f=1 no=1). What decimal value does out have?
questions.explain: y becomes !20 = -21. f = 1 gives 30 + (-21) = 9. no = 1 gives !9 = -10. This row computes y - x = 20 - 30 = -10.

questions.q: When the ALU outputs out = -10, what are zr and ng?
choices: zr = 0, ng = 1
zr = 1, ng = 1
zr = 0, ng = 0
zr = 1, ng = 0
questions.explain: zr = 1 only if out = 0, and ng = 1 only if out < 0. -10 is nonzero and negative.

questions.q: In the Hack ALU, f = 1 selects x&y and f = 0 selects x+y.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: f = 1 means out = x + y (two's complement addition), and f = 0 means out = x & y (bit-wise And).

questions.q: Using 4-bit values x = 0101 (5) and y = 0011 (3), what 4-bit output does the ALU produce for control bits 010011?
questions.explain: nx = 1 gives x = 1010. y stays 0011. f = 1 gives 1010 + 0011 = 1101. no = 1 gives 0010 = 2, which is x - y = 5 - 3.

questions.q: How do the control bits 001100 make the ALU output x?
choices: y is zeroed and then negated into all 1s, and f = 0 computes x & 111...1 = x
y is zeroed, and f = 1 computes x + 0 = x
x is negated twice, once by nx and once by no
f = 0 bypasses y and passes x straight through
questions.explain: zy = 1 and ny = 1 turn y into 111...1. f = 0 Ands: x & 111...1 = x. no = 0. Zeroing y and adding would also give x, but these bits have ny = 1 and f = 0, which means And with all 1s.

questions.q: Which of these are among the 18 documented Hack ALU functions?
choices: y-x
x|y
x*y
!y
x Xor y
questions.explain: The 18 are: 0, 1, -1, x, y, !x, !y, -x, -y, x+1, y+1, x-1, y-1, x+y, x-y, y-x, x&y, x|y. The ALU has no multiplication and no Xor function.

questions.q: The Hack ALU detects arithmetic overflow and reports it on the ng output.
questions.explain: Overflow is neither detected nor handled. ng only reports whether out < 0, i.e., whether the MSB of out is 1.

questions.q: Which identity explains the ALU's -x row (control bits 001111)?
choices: -x = !x

questions.q: Which identity explains the ALU's x+1 row (control bits 011111)?
questions.explain: nx makes x = !x, zy and ny make y = -1, f adds, and no negates: !(!x - 1). Example with x = 1001 (-7): !x = 0110, 0110 + 1111 = (1)0101, !0101 = 1010 = -6 = x + 1.

questions.q: Use the identity x - y = !(!x + y) on 4-bit values x = 0010 (2) and y = 1011 (-5). Give the 4-bit result.
questions.explain: !x = 1101. 1101 + 1011 = (1)1000, and dropping the overflow bit leaves 1000. !1000 = 0111 = 7, which equals 2 - (-5).

questions.q: When implementing the ALU, the ng output (out < 0) can be taken directly from:
choices: out[15], the most significant bit of out
out[0], the least significant bit of out
An Or of all 16 bits of out
An And of all 16 bits of out
questions.explain: In two's complement every negative number's code starts with 1, so out < 0 exactly when the MSB, out[15], is 1.

questions.q: Which logic correctly computes the ALU's zr output (zr = 1 iff out == 0)?
choices: Not of an Or over all 16 bits of out
An And over all 16 bits of out
Not(out[15])
out[0]
questions.explain: out is 0 only when every bit is 0. An Or over all bits is 1 if any bit is 1, so negating it gives 1 exactly when all bits are 0.

questions.q: Deciding which functions the ALU should compute is a hardware/software trade-off. Which statement describes it?
choices: Hardware implementations are faster but more expensive; software implementations are slower but less expensive
Hardware implementations are slower but cheaper; software implementations are faster but more expensive
Hardware and software implementations cost the same, but hardware is faster
Functions left out of the ALU can never be computed
questions.explain: Functions the ALU does not implement can be added later in software. Hack chooses a simple ALU and leaves the rest to software.

questions.q: The Hack ALU has no multiplication, division, or floating-point arithmetic; these are meant to be implemented in software (at the operating-system level).
questions.explain: The design keeps the ALU hardware limited and does as much as possible in software. Multiplication and division can be built efficiently out of addition.

questions.q: z is an 8-bit bus connected in a part as: chipPart(..., z[0..2]=true, z[6..7]=true). Write the value of z from bit 7 down to bit 0.
questions.explain: Bits 0-2 and 6-7 are set to 1. Unassigned bits (3, 4, 5) default to 0. Reading from bit 7 to bit 0: 11000111.

questions.q: In HDL, how do you connect a 16-bit input pin x of a chip part to the constant 0000000000000000?
choices: x=false
x=true
x[0]=false
questions.explain: false is the all-0s constant and true is the all-1s constant for a pin or bus of any width. x[0]=false only names bit 0 (the other bits would also default to 0, but x=false is the direct way).

questions.q: Inside a chip with 8-bit inputs x and y, what does Add16(a[0..7]=x, a[8..15]=y, b=z, out=...) do?
choices: Builds Add16's a input with x as its low 8 bits and y as its high 8 bits
Adds x and y and stores the 16-bit result in a
Builds a with y as its low 8 bits and x as its high 8 bits
Is invalid, because 8-bit buses cannot connect to a 16-bit pin
questions.explain: Sub-bussing lets you assign n-bit values to slices of a bus. Bit 0 is the LSB, so a[0..7] = x is the low half and a[8..15] = y is the high half.

questions.q: Writing out[0..3]=t1 in a chip part's connections creates a 4-bit internal pin t1 that carries the low 4 bits of the part's output.
questions.explain: You can create internal bus pins of any width n by connecting them to a sub-bus of a part's output. Here t1 gets bits 0-3 of out.
